passages.title: Passage A: Constructive vs. Classical Negation
passages.body: In intuitionistic type theory (as implemented in Lean 4's core), ¬P is defined as P → False. Under this definition, the implication ¬(P ∨ Q) → ¬P ∧ ¬Q is constructively provable without using the Law of Excluded Middle (LEM). By contrast, deriving ¬P ∨ ¬Q from ¬(P ∧ Q) requires classical reasoning because knowing that P and Q cannot both hold does not constructively tell us which one fails. Similarly, while (P → Q) → (¬Q → ¬P) is constructive, its converse (¬Q → ¬P) → (P → Q) requires double-negation elimination.

items.stem: Why is ¬(P ∨ Q) → ¬P ∧ ¬Q provable constructively in Lean 4?

options.A: Because Lean 4 enables LEM by default in its core
options.B: Because ¬P is P → False and each disjunct injects directly into P ∨ Q
options.C: Because ∧ and ∨ are identical in type theory

items.explanation: Constructive proofs of ¬P and ¬Q only need Or.inl/Or.inr and h : (P ∨ Q) → False.

items.stem: Which implication in the passage requires classical reasoning?
items.explanation: Constructively, knowing ¬(P ∧ Q) does not decide which of P or Q fails.

items.stem: What extra principle is needed for (¬Q → ¬P) → (P → Q)?
items.explanation: The passage states the converse of contraposition requires double-negation elimination.

part3.passage:
Theorem: For any propositions P and Q, ¬(P ∨ Q) → ¬P ∧ ¬Q.

options.text: Assume h : ¬(P ∨ Q), meaning any proof of P ∨ Q yields False.
To prove the conjunction ¬P ∧ ¬Q, split into two subgoals: ¬P and ¬Q.
For the first subgoal ¬P, assume hp : P and form Or.inl hp : P ∨ Q, then apply h to obtain False.
For the second subgoal ¬Q, assume hq : Q and form Or.inr hq : P ∨ Q, then apply h to obtain False.
Combining both subgoals completes the proof of ¬P ∧ ¬Q.
Invoke the Law of Excluded Middle on P to split into cases P and ¬P.
Assume ¬P ∧ ¬Q and derive P ∨ Q by modus ponens.

items.explanation: To prove an implication, first introduce its antecedent h : ¬(P ∨ Q).
Next decompose the conjunction goal ¬P ∧ ¬Q into two subgoals.
Prove ¬P by injecting hp into P ∨ Q via Or.inl and applying h.
Prove ¬Q symmetrically using Or.inr.
Once both conjuncts are proved, the theorem is established.

distractorExplanations.F: LEM is unnecessary; this direction of De Morgan's Law is purely constructive.
distractorExplanations.G: This reverses the implication direction and assumes the conclusion.

part4.passage: To prove (P → Q) → (¬Q → ¬P), we first [1] hPQ : P → Q. Next we assume hnotQ : ¬Q and hp : P. Applying hPQ to hp produces a proof of [2]. Because ¬Q is definitionally Q → [3], applying hnotQ to that proof yields a contradiction. Note that if we instead tried to prove (P → Q) → (Q → P), the claim would be [4] in general, since Q being true does not force P to hold. Likewise, negating ∀ x, P x yields ∃ x, [5], whereas negating ∃ x, P x yields [6] x, ¬P x.

part7.prompt: Prove De Morgan's Law constructively in Lean 4 without using sorry, admit, or custom axioms. Keep the exact theorem signature unchanged. Also answer the 2 quick verification checks below.
part7.starterCode:
theorem de_morgan_or (P Q : Prop) : ¬(P ∨ Q) → ¬P ∧ ¬Q :=
  by
    sorry
part7.referenceSolution:
theorem de_morgan_or (P Q : Prop) : ¬(P ∨ Q) → ¬P ∧ ¬Q :=
  by
    intro h
    constructor
    · exact fun hp => h (Or.inl hp)
    · exact fun hq => h (Or.inr hq)
part7.negativeSolution:
theorem de_morgan_or (P Q : Prop) : ¬(P ∨ Q) → ¬P ∧ ¬Q :=
  by
    sorry
